It’s really strange to suddenly be awakened to a sense of how temporary the civilization I was (am, as of now) living in is. As with all things, I knew it as a fact but have only really begun to understand it recently. The time will pass, and through that very fact the world will not stay the same. As humanity now is only the current crest of the wave on the entire ocean of humanity or the existence of the world/universe in general, we will quickly and seamlessly be replaced by the next crest, and the next. Not the next wave - the foam will dissolve and tumble to make way for new foam right there, still on the crest of the very same wave. One would only need to see a picture of the world in 1000 years, or just 100, to see how temporary the time they’re currently living in is.
But I’m getting too logical. Fundamentally I am just really taken by the understanding of how large a time scale things will go on for, and how the collective consciousness of humanity changes as a whole. Yes, humanity will end in a pathetic whimpering tantrum of screens and outrage and politics; this current iteration of humanity will. But all things will not end just because the current form humanity takes is doomed. There will be more humans born after the bombs. One hundred winters will pass. Something new will begin. Things for me have only ever felt like the end of everything because I assumed that what I knew was the unchanging everything, and for humanity as I was accustomed to it since being a child ended was for “everything” to end. But no - I will, despite my primitive understanding, live through the changing on an epoch. I will be one of the ones to say that things aren’t like they used to be - not in a minute “things are still operating how they used to but only much smaller, much more aggravated, much more shortsighted” but instead as a large “the conduct of humanity has fundamentally changed since I was young”. There is continuous change and there is, still, simultaneously, the change of borders and whiplash and abrupt cutoffs, which happen seldom but deliberately. Changes where everyone who lived through it remember it with unbearable poignancy, and that those born after the change will be unable to see why the way things were mattered so much to us until they perhaps live through a similar change themselves. 
And that is something that I don’t know will happen, not so quickly. It will happen again eventually, the universe and path of everything is simply a series of bubbling-overs and dying downs and reignitings. But even living through one change does not mean I know them all, and does not mean I know when the next one will happen. Intuitively, however, I feel that a change of the magnitude I am expecting happens seldom, once something has been around long enough to accumulate enough slag to discharge in one vibrant shock.

I almost worry, in a cosmic sense, that me speedrunning an acceptance of death means I will die soon. Or what, I accept death and live 40 more years anyway?? I imagine accepting death, truly, is precipitated by the actual decline into death. Unless of course death is an accident, which is almost what I imagine is the death that awaits a healthy person who accepts death early in life. Which is why I worry I will die in some sort of accident. The 2028 bombings, perhaps?

I think the reason you have to pay attention to life is because life changes, and you don’t get to go back and revisit parts. I mean this, of course, in the obvious way of “you will lose things and people so cherish them while you have them etc etc”. But I also mean this in the general sense that you only get to be young and clueless once. At a certain point, you will begin to accumulate enough experience that you are no longer “new” to the world, in the sense of a human lifespan. You will no longer feel like a beginner to the things around you; you will be intermediate. And you cannot go back. once you stand up and start walking, you cannot stop walking. Once you learn fundamentals, you can’t unlearn them. Once you are accustomed to how your life feels, and begin to form connections based off of that feeling, you cannot go back to when the feeling was new. Once you have encountered the “beginner hurdles” and have fallen flat on your face at the starting line enough times, you will find yourself suddenly past the hurdles.

A lot of what I would call “immature” creations, namely those surrounding making characters and putting them in adverse situations/showing them distressed, annoyed, hurt, etc. just for the sake of doing so, essentially normalize the outward expression of emotions, but not the inward experience of them. Ultimately it gives “the group engaging in those creations” an excuse to not manage these emotions because it becomes seen almost as desirable to be “real” and display these emotions, but there is very little focus on what it’s really like to be a human being experiencing the emotions, which means nobody in “the group” actually learns how to maintain themselves in the face of really horrible feelings, or even simple undesireable ones. It’s one thing to look at an animation of a character poking their head out, looking annoyed or dismayed at the rain, and going back inside - it’s an entirely separate thing to feel the frustration and depression and stooped-under-a-ceiling feeling that you get with something like that, and so whenever someone in that group feels anything like that it remains just as unbearable as it was before they saw the animation.
Okay that sounded really hater-y. I guess the point I’m really trying to get at is that it completely misses subjective internal lived experiences, and focuses only on the external representation of those experiences. which I guess is just a rephrasing of the last part of this entry’s topic sentence. But the belief that that form of emotional expression IS the experience of the emotion being portrayed is completely incorrect because it’s formulated entirely within the sphere of codified emotions such as “sad, annoyed,” and other such concrete and arbitrary labels (and their popular societal representations) rather than dealing with the nuanced beyond-words experience of the actual moment being portrayed. A clarification of the previous entry. It’s not that the art you make that you don’t show anybody isn’t important, isn’t meaningful, isn’t part of who you are. But it is only meaningful and important to yourself. incidentally, the effect the art has on you will trickle out into the world via your actions and outlook being influence by it, and your actions/outlook subsequently influencing other things, but the bulk of its importance is entirely contained within you. And to really understand this requires understanding fully the other concept, that to other people you are only how you appear to them and interact with them. You, in your “whole self”, are not given to other people; you only give them exactly what you give them. if you don’t show parts of yourself to other people, then those parts of yourself don’t exist to other people, flat.

An act of creation is not done when the creation is finished; it is completed only when it is shown. If I make really crazy art, but I keep it to myself and never show it, I don’t get to claim that that art is a true reflection of me. It is only when I show the pieces to others that it becomes part of me, as far as the world is concerned, which is the one and only concerned party. A musician that never releases their best tracks is a musician that doesn’t have any good tracks. The expression of an emotion/experience is the completion of the emotion/experience; expression is not supplemental, it is part of the thing itself. I have many works I have never shown, and those are the ones I consider incomplete. This whole journal thing is, in my mind, one huge incomplete thing, because I haven’t shown it to anybody. And, as a side note, putting it n my website hardly counts; I know nobody reads that shit.

I think rain is also so cool because it is just tiny specks of water. Virtually everywhere else in life, water is seen as a group - in bottles, in puddles, coming from faucets, in bowls or pots, in rivers, in oceans. A lot of water clumps together. You only really see small pieces of water in the shower, or the sparse occasions where water splashes for some unknown reason, and you witness droplets fly for only a brief imprint of time. Rain is really the only substantial thing in life where you see, sustained, many many tiny water droplets. The air is not 100% water, there is actually (in a general comparative sense) still very little water in the air around you; there are just so many of them on TOP of each other that everything gets soaked as though thoroughly doused with a steady solid stream. It gives a latent sense of verticality to the wetness on everything, because there must have been so many rain drops falling on top of each other to make the surroundings so thoroughly drenched since each individual drop only wets such a small area.

I don’t burn bridges, I just walk away from them. 
Historically, I have never burned bridges, and the closest I have come has been with coercion. I never press the button to detonate or light the match. 
I imagine there is something at least final about a burned bridge, about seeing a canyon with nothing above it. I imagine there is a whole host of other emotions of unique grief and regret that I am not often privvy to that must come with said finality, but at least there is no indecision or hesitancy there.
But there is a whole different weight in approaching the cliff and seeing a bridge still standing there, intact, albeit fallen into disrepair. 
It is a much more worldly loneliness, because the grief is no longer contained to this one area, by the very fact that the bridge is still standing. It’s not that you can’t reach the other side, but that to do so would be pointless, because the other side is empty. After you left, so too did they.
It is not too difficult to simply turn around while a bridge is in use and suddenly stop using it anymore, unfortunately - it is a cowardly thing to do. And it leaves you with the eternal weight of the abandoned bridge forever.
It is such a heavy weight to carry around. I cannot even have the relief of having the weight of wood planks and ropes stripped from hull and fall away. The bridges stay there, in their full weight, and accumulate more by their heaviness in the landscape and by the emotions that pile up, brought as boulders in my shaking arms only to be dropped at the base, because I forget again and again that there is nobody to carry them across to anymore. My ritualistic mind continues, by habit and hope, again and again to prepare for the journey across. It is difficult to see nothing preventing you from stepping foot onto the bridge, but nevertheless restraining yourself to sit down and weep quickly before the foundation. It is difficult to know that you are the only thing stopping yourself from crossing, regardless of “how mature” you are or not for being able to do so - to know you cannot pin your grief on anything or anyone besides yourself, and the entirety of the air around you.
Air which, mind you, does not stagnate. The bridge is not necessarily full of fresh air and oxygen, but it is not stuffy; it is simply completely still, and shows obvious signs of age and decay. Even if this bridge was once in use, the very fact that it has been in disrepair for so long is proof enough that it doesn’t matter if it’s still standing or not; it leads nowhere, and hasn’t for ages, and any reason for its existence which once flitted across and at its ends has long since disappeared.
It now sits simply to remind you that it is there. 
Having a bridge become a centerpoint, rather than remaining a vessel between the two centerpoints it was originally made to connect, is a heartbreakingly solemn sight.
//////
Historically, these bridges have sat in my mind in one gut wrenching bucket of “things that I could go back to”, sitting in the corner of my brain collecting dust but still very very very felt. A bucket that, since I haven’t technically burned the bridges inside of it, I could return to, and I could cross that bridge again, and I could meet that other person on the other side again (note: i can’t do this in practice, but by not looking, I can pretend I can). And I would never visit the bridges again because, ultimately I was scared for what I would find. I am terrible at returns from absences; they terrify me. Once I have said goodbye to somebody, I don’t look back - at least not in action. I step away my side of the bridge and walk away, but keep thinking ABOUT the bridge and what’s on the other side - or, what was on the other side. What was on the other side when I was there that is no longer there, or has changed.
It is even more terrifying when it is somebody that knows me. Not somebody who will turn around when I call their name, but will turn around when they see me. I will be known walking back in.
My mind is really averse to interacting with the conflicted area where the past abruptly jumps to something in the future. And yet I am so interested in the experience OF the conflict itself. I tell myself I should feel bad about this, because it is disrespecting the person on the other side to be continually poking at a memory that isn’t them anymore. But I don’t think that’s true. I think focusing on what is there is the only thing I can do truly; focus on coming terms to it. 
I wonder if I am too absorbed in my own conflicts to be able to communicate clearly to others.

But it IS effort - you have to remain contentious and aware of what they are doing, and how you feel about it, to be able to truly interact with them. I cannot just “follow the woke patterns” I figured out, because there is no pattern, except on a scale that you cannot meaningfully act upon in small local conversations.
Essentially, I made the realization that you have to stop policing yourself so much to act “true to yourself” i.e. “like an actual human being” but I accidentally fell into a trap of “that means I don’t have to put effort in”, which is a very logical conclusion to reach. It takes the assumption that “trying” to do something is ultimately against what you naturally would have done, and comes to the conclusion that therefor you should stop trying. But that’s completely false - natural action involves trying, it just can’t be trying that you arbitrarily enforce on yourself!
While it’s true that it’s arbitrary and ultimately unnecessary for me to try and “replicate” the behavior of those more well adjusted than me, I nevertheless still have to try to improve myself if I’m going to become “as well adjusted”, I can’t simply sit back and say “nature will take me there :)” because I forget that I influence nature, and by sitting back and doing nothing, I am commanding nature to atrophy!

A different way to phrase the idea of the previous entries on death. I am increasingly coming to terms with the relative unchangingness of the location and feel of my consciousness. The realization that regardless of what events happen in my life or what I go through, they do always pass, and I always implicitly return to the same quiet still center that I have found myself in uncountable times before. As incredible as new experiences are, they have never changed my entire life. I have never, as I said before, stepped into a “Universe 2” after experiencing anything. Even as transformative as experiences have been, it becomes obvious looking back that I was in the same world as I always had been both before and after.
I think about the prospect of the experiences I will be missing when I die. Of all the things I never would have gotten to do, all the extremes and highlights that I will never know. And I increasingly see that whether I experience them or not, my death will not change. 
Just the same as dreams and distant memories live in my head in the same way as each other but do not substantially change my lived experience as it is right now, so too do any extreme experiences I could have not substantially change me afterwards, or at the moment of my death. The experience of a quiet day, looking at leaves in the wind, is forever its own small universe to enter.
Before, I suppose I said that because of my love of the uniqueness of every experience, that’s exactly why I wanted to experience extremes - so I could know what the spikes are that I would never touch before. But now that same love is what makes me okay with not experiencing them – or will make me completely accepting of whatever experiences I did or did not have when I am at the moment of my death.
Giving myself up on a quiet day by myself will not feel different if I got to swing over a canyon or fly, somehow, through the air. In the best way possible, I have always always always and will always always always return to the median that is “having a lived experience”.
In more logical terms, I am beginning to feel my life as one string of experience, as a whole that is entirely greater and something other than the sum of its parts, rather than “merely” the collection of bright color beads of experience that make it up. I feel some overarching continuous through line that extends through it all, and will remain regardless of what beads get added - and prospectively will end the same.

I have long figured how I would want to die, and my idea has always been something brave and grand. I’ve wanted to go out with some hurrah - jumping off a plane without a parachute, something - to get one last experience I never could have gotten while alive, if I had hoped to keep living afterwards.
This is the first time I don’t want that. Having my life end in a culmination of a long ascent, thumping rotors, scream-muffled voices, whipping wind - it sounds absurdly overwhelming. I would hardly be able to meet my death if my acceptance of it was beaten out of me by gale force winds tearing at my face.
I think, now, I understand why people want to die in the most banal way possible; laying in bed. I do want to be comfortable, quiet, and still when I meet the long sonorous note of death. I want to experience the full drawing out of my consciousness into one impossibly long and thin thread, to feel the promised transformative rest finally take me. I want to be able to give myself up.

Thinking about the switchover from learning a system to learning how to manipulate a system. For example; Rain World. I am still mulling over the switch I had from “being amazed at the world I was in, feeling much smaller than it, exploring as a small creature” to “oh I got this now, let me try this and that, I wonder if I could…” etc. That sort of mindset shift is present in nearly any new thing I devote myself to, be that a new browser based particle system game or a new programming language. For example, there is a point in the beginning of the particle sim where I am not really “doing anything” with it. I am simply clicking on this new particle or that one, letting them fall, and seeing what happens. I lump as many as I can together to see what happens. A similar thing happened when I played Noita too. When I started playing Noita, I was immensely scared of the world, I had no idea what was going to happen or what *could* happen. I did runs purely to take in the experience of what the world was like and just to see what *things* were in it. But after a certain point, I hit the phase when I just threw as many mods together as I could. This of course completely broke the cohesive immersion that the game created for itself, but added a whole lot more unexpectedness. What I was chasing when I did this wasn’t mastery or understanding or knowledge, it was simply more of the “wow wtf is all this I’m scared of it” feeling. In Rain World, after I did my first run through, the first thing I did was to immediately download every single region mod I could find and string them together so I could visit every single one, regardless of which regions were supposed to fit together and if they complemented the base game or not.
This is to say, I am very much beginning to a see a pattern in my relation to learning “systems” for the first time. I start and I am awed and humbled by the system and my lack of knowledge in it → as soon as I begin to get a modicum of understanding, I do everything in my power to crank the processes of the system up to 10 purely for the experience of it → (I get bored and stop playing the thing for a little while) → I come back and give myself a much more “vanilla” experience, but with meaningful and thoughtful tweaks provided by the experiences before (those being less “intelligent experiences I got while playing” and more “holistic changes that are simply meant to enhance the base experience instead of change it”) → (I do not have many data points for whether this phase exists or not, but I can only imagine it does) creating my own process within the system from scratch.
I include that last one because this whole step by step process seems very much like a learning creators arc, and I can only imagine all this theory crafting and tinkering ultimately ends with a custom creation. The only real thing i can put this to right now is my time with Procreate and/or visual art in general, if I am able to follow the same loose outline. I started drawing, and was amazed by how much I could do → I started doing hella edits and extreme color saturation → I got frustrated and didn’t really know “what else I could do” → I have gone back and now create things in a much more modest way (i.e. I only use the parts of the editor I know I need/want, rather than simply using parts to use them)

And I would look back and be frustrated with myself that I couldn’t “control” myself, that I kept “imposing understanding and technical manipulation” onto processes that in my head I “wanted to remain processes”
It is as though I refused to acknowledge to myself the personal value of experimentation and trying to manipulate a system. As thought I viewed the start of my learning arc - the start of any learning arc, the “cluelessly but fearlessly fucking around” phase - as a personal failure, as a sign of mediocrity and a limited attention span.
Which, looking on it now, not only seems silly but also illuminates to myself so much of my approach to the world, and what I couldn’t figure out for a while. I think I implicitly figured it out a while ago and tried to put words to it many times, but I never really could. I had this idea of purity or sanctity of systems, that they should be appreciated simply for what they are and that anything I did to them was unecessary. Not trivial per se, but I thought that for me to try and manipulate the system was essentially to not be fully appreciating or respecting the system, which I viewed as a personal failing. I viewed it as me “not being able” to divorce myself from my urges enough (a lot of this came from the buddhist and zen texts I read around the time I was struggling with this problem) and that whatever I created would be no more or less amazing than what was already there. And the fact that my mind follows this pattern over and over and over again with so many different new things I immerse myself into - Noita, Rain World, drawing, etc - should prove to me how base and essential and natural it is!
There certainly are things to be learned from “being able to” appreciate a system as is, and recognize when there is no need for you to mess around with them. Even if, somehow (I do not say this out of hope, but out of clarity) she were to come back into my life, it would not be to the same room; too much time has passed. A new room would be created to hold her.
That room, and many others like it, will forever remain empty. From their point of view, my back will forever be turned, I will forever be entering other rooms and turning my life and activity towards others. It will exist near the end of a growing litany of deprecated and abandoned rooms.
I don’t know how to feel about this. So many of these rooms I don’t even remember my way back to. So many I have lost the key to. So many I didn’t say goodbye to; I simply left one day, and never came back. I’m conflicted about this; the thought of going years and years still not looking at them, of dying and leaving them still completely dilapidated and desolate, seems wrong; but so does the idea of intentionally revisiting them just for the sake of saying I saw them one last time.

An entire life’s worth of experiences is a heavy burden however old I am, and only gets heavier as I keep getting older. I must make sure I do not break my back attempting to carry every ounce of it every day.
Not to say that reflecting on the past = “living in the past” = bad; I’m assuming I’ve far more often than enough gone over why I think reflecting on the past is important. But it also, sometimes, is very important to forget the past too. I find myself more and more rarely allowing myself to live the day as is, without the “cache” of my entire life hovering around the corners of my vision.
And I think this only makes it harder and harder to keep moving forward and creating new things. Of course, drawing from past experiences is exactly what helps me create, but too much time spent living in the past blots out any present or future with which I can create in the first place; and likewise, regardless of how directly something I make is related to some past experience of mine, the thing I create and the process of creating it live in the present onward, not in the past. Every moment in the past is a moment I am not moving forward.
To sit and make sure that I savour every moment of my life - to the extent that I try to keep it all in my memory, and not forget any of it - I end up manufacturing for myself a crushing weight of nostalgia and examples of how my current life is NOT whatever it was in the past, which in turn naturally lends itself to the “well I should make it like the past” instead of the oft preferred “that’s fine :)”. Regardless of how well adjusted I am, more time thinking about the past often simply implicitly makes me wish for the past again, and lament to some degree or another that it’s not like that anymore.
I can only imagine that thinking about the past makes it harder and harder to create new things. As I get older, I think more and more and more about the life that I have lived. I am not sure what to do about this, or if I can; rather, I’m not sure what to make of it. All I know is that as I get more and more and more experiences piled on to me, I end up thinking about all of them. And I can only imagine that at some point, I need to be okay with forgetting my own life if I am to live it properly.

I think I’m forgoing the standard bullet-point way I’ve been doing these entries, and I’ll instead start doing paragraphs. A boon to some and a bane to others. We will see if I stay this way. I personally have some qualms with paragraphs, as I feel they are difficult to read on computer screens. From a more selfish perspective, I fear that making my writing into paragraphs somehow takes away some of the intimacy, and/or makes readers disinterested.

In some form, despite this not being my intention, paragraphs seem less individual. Without my realizing it, I had kind of come to see my bullet-point style of writing as somehow distinctive, as setting me apart from others, as something of a “selling point” about me that others did not have; all the “paragraph writers” were lumped together and my writing stood apart by virtue of it’s structure. And now that I am writing paragraphs, I don’t have that anymore, and am forced to confront that I, just like every other blogger and writer and scrawler, am simply writing words for myself with no particular mastery.

Something feels blasphemous about making any analogy or comparison that involves technology. Or, when attempting to make an observation of the world around me, acknowledging a computer screen or calculator. It feels as though they are blips in the world that I should look over, they are living abstractions from what I should “really” focus on that are false bases for attention; any attempt to categorize them as part of the simple and natural world as presented to you feels like it somehow ignores this pocket dimension contained within the object. I cannot acknowledge the entirety of the internet within my room, so it would be a lie to attempt to acknowledge “only” the computer screen.
